items.reason: This is the reported cancel hole: before the fix any signed-in user could cancel any order. Functional because the check spans the API, query and database.

items.title: Bob cannot cancel alice's cancellable Submitted order

items.title: Cancelling an unknown order returns the same 404 as a not-owned order
covers: Decision: 404 for orders the caller does not own and for orders that do not exist
items.reason: The decision is that callers must not tell the two cases apart; a different status or body would leak which order numbers exist.

items.title: Owner can still cancel their own Submitted order
covers: Cancel of own order still returns 200
items.reason: Guards against a fix that rejects every cancel. Proves the ownership check passes for the owner.

items.title: Buyer alice cannot ship bob's Paid order; 403 and order unchanged
items.reason: This is the exact reproduction in the story (alice ships order 7). A buyer must be stopped by the Admin policy before the endpoint runs.

items.title: Buyer cannot ship even their own Paid order
covers: Shipping limited to a back-office role, not buyers
items.reason: The story says shipping is a back-office action, not just an ownership matter. Order 4 is alice's own Paid order, so only the role check can reject it.

items.title: Admin can ship any buyer's Paid order
items.reason: Positive counterpart of the role rule: the back-office role must still ship, including orders it does not own as a buyer.

items.title: Admin shipping an unknown order number gets 404
covers: Decision: admin shipping an unknown order gets 404
items.reason: Covers the new existence check; before it, an unknown order failed differently. Admin is used so the role gate is passed.

items.title: Buyer shipping with an empty x-requestid gets 403, not 400
covers: Decision: buyer with empty x-requestid gets 403 before the endpoint runs
items.reason: Records the changed behavior: the role gate runs before request-id validation. Without this case the old 400 could silently return.

items.title: Admin shipping with an empty x-requestid still gets 400
covers: Decision: admins still get 400 for empty x-requestid
items.reason: Request-id validation must still work for the role that reaches the endpoint.

items.title: Cancel and ship without a token return 401

items.reason: The new policy must not weaken authentication; a fix that only added role handling could still let anonymous calls through the cancel endpoint.

items.title: Cancelling a Shipped order returns 409 with the rule message
items.reason: This is the exact reproduction in the bug report; it returned 500 before. Functional layer because the status mapping and the domain rule only meet in the running API with a real database.

items.title: Cancelling a Paid order returns 409 with the rule message
items.reason: SetCancelledStatus rejects Paid as well as Shipped; a second source status proves the mapping is generic and not tied to one status.

items.title: Shipping a Submitted order returns 409 with the rule message
items.reason: The ship endpoint has its own 500 mapping, so cancel being fixed does not prove ship is. Submitted is the unpaid source status used by the existing e2e test.

items.title: Shipping a Cancelled order returns 409 with the rule message
items.reason: A terminal status other than Shipped, so the ship mapping is not special-cased to one status.

items.title: Shipping an already Shipped order returns 409 with the rule message
items.reason: Shipping twice is a plausible real user mistake and was listed as an invalid transition in the existing e2e test.

items.title: A rejected status change leaves the order unchanged
covers: Implementation Notes: rethrown domain error rolls back the outer transaction
items.reason: Rethrowing from the idempotency wrapper must not persist a partial change; this checks the rollback by reading the order afterwards.

items.title: Retrying a rejected change with the same x-requestid returns 409 again
covers: Implementation Notes: request id is not recorded, retry gets the same 409
items.reason: The wrapper used to swallow the error and a duplicate id then looked like success. The story states a retry now gets the same 409; the risk is a silent 200 on retry.

items.title: Cancelling an unknown order returns 404
covers: Suggested fix: return 404 when the order does not exist
items.reason: The fix must not turn the existing not-found path into 409 or 500. Order 999 does not exist in the scenario.

items.title: Shipping an unknown order returns 404
covers: Suggested fix: return 404 when the order does not exist
items.reason: Ship has a separate existence check from cancel; it needs its own check.

items.title: Cancelling another buyer's order returns 404, not 409
covers: Implementation Notes: other buyers' orders keep 404
items.reason: Order 7 is Paid, so a naive implementation that skips the ownership check would answer 409 and leak that the order exists and its status.

items.title: Shipping as a non-Admin still returns 403
covers: Implementation Notes: ship by non-Admin keeps 403 from OrderingAdmin policy
items.reason: The authorization policy runs before the handler; the case guards that the new 409 mapping does not change the order of checks. Order 4 is Paid, so shipping would otherwise succeed.

items.title: Cancelling a Submitted order still returns 200 and cancels it
items.reason: Guards against the fix over-mapping errors; the success path goes through the changed idempotency wrapper.

items.title: Shipping a Paid order as admin still returns 200 and ships it
items.reason: Same as the cancel regression for the ship endpoint. Order 7 is used so the case does not depend on order 4, which other cases only read.
